summary: A 1976 paper suggesting extensions to the simple Procedure Call Protocol described earlier. By expanding the procedure call model and standardising other forms of inter-process interaction, it aims to give programmers a more powerful distributed programming system.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 708 expands a remote procedure-call model with ways for distributed programs to create and introduce processes, control access to groups of procedures, and share data. It presents these mechanisms as proposals for further research.

questions: what does rfc 708 add to remote procedure calls
how can distributed processes be introduced
how does rfc 708 propose controlling package access
subtitle: Proposed extensions to a remote procedure-call model for distributed programs.

tldr.problem: A basic remote procedure call lets one process invoke a procedure on another, but distributed programs may also need process creation, introductions, access controls, shared variables, and richer interactions.
tldr.mechanism: The paper proposes system procedures that runtime environments use to create processes, connect them, manage packages and variables, and support signalling, help, notification, and cancellation.
tldr.outcome: The author offers these extensions as research ideas to make the distributed programming system more capable, not as a final specification.

today: RFC 708 presents proposed extensions to a distributed programming system and says they are intended to stimulate further research. The conclusion notes that additional forms of process interaction remain to be explored.

sections.title: Beyond a Basic Remote Call
sections.content:
The earlier Procedure Call Protocol lets one process name a procedure on a distant process, provide arguments, and receive an outcome and results. RFC 708 argues that this supports only basic request-and-return interactions.

The proposed additions are system procedures used by runtime environments. They extend the facilities available to applications while leaving the basic call protocol as the foundation.
sections.plainLanguage: A remote call lets one program ask another to run a procedure and return a result. This paper asks what other operations distributed programs need.

sections.title: Managing Processes and Connections
sections.content:
The proposed CRTPROCESS primitive creates a process on a remote computer or establishes contact with one, returning a process handle. DELPROCESS ends the association. The paper also proposes introducing two processes so they can call each other's procedures.

When the processes cannot share one inter-process communication facility, a logical channel can relay messages through intermediate processes. The runtime environments handle that relaying.
sections.plainLanguage: A program could ask a remote computer to start or contact a process. Two processes could be introduced, with intermediate processes relaying messages when needed.

sections.title: Packages and Shared Variables
sections.content:
The paper proposes grouping related procedures into packages. A process opens a package and receives a package handle before calling procedures in it; opening the package provides a point where access can be checked.

It also proposes named shared variables with read and write procedures. Optional masks could let procedure results remain in the callee's process for a later call, or be discarded instead of sent back.
sections.plainLanguage: A package groups procedures so access can be checked when the group is opened. Shared variables and optional parameter handling are proposed to support data exchange.

sections.title: Richer Procedure Interactions
sections.content:
Additional proposed procedures let a caller and callee transfer control, send signals while a call remains active, ask a superior process for help, report events to superiors, or abort a procedure.

The conclusion calls the expanded set a coherent set of tools for constructing distributed systems, while noting that other forms of process interaction remain to be explored.
sections.plainLanguage: The proposals also cover longer conversations than one call and reply. A process could hand control back and forth, request help, report an event, or cancel a call.
